title: På flyplassen / At the Airport
bridge: In Norwegian, unlike English, the word for 'airport' is 'flyplass' (or 'flyplassen' in definite form), which directly translates to 'air place'. When asking for directions or services, Norwegians often use the verb 'å få' (to get) instead of 'to have' or 'to need', which can be confusing for English speakers. Additionally, Norwegian speakers tend to be more direct in their requests, so phrases like 'Kan du hjelpe meg?' (Can you help me?) are common and polite.
rule: To ask for directions or services at the airport, use the phrase 'Unnskyld, kan du hjelpe meg?' (Excuse me, can you help me?). For specific requests, use 'Hvor er...?' (Where is...?) followed by the location. To express gratitude, say 'Takk' (Thanks) or 'Takk skal du ha' (Thank you very much). Remember, Norwegian sentences often follow the Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) order, similar to English, but word order can change in questions.

title: Å bestille et hotellrom / Booking a Hotel Room
bridge: In Norwegian, the verb 'å bestille' is used for booking a hotel room, similar to 'to book' in English. However, Norwegian often uses the preposition 'et' for 'a' before masculine nouns like 'hotellrom', which is different from English. Be careful with word order in questions, as Norwegian typically places the verb second in main clauses, unlike English.
rule: To book a hotel room in Norwegian, use the phrase 'Å bestille et hotellrom'. The verb 'å bestille' is followed by the object 'et hotellrom'. In questions, the word order changes to V2 (verb second), e.g., 'Kan jeg bestille et hotellrom?' (Can I book a hotel room?). Remember to use 'et' for masculine nouns like 'hotellrom'.

title: Bestille mat / Ordering Food
bridge: In Norwegian, ordering food involves using the verb 'å bestille,' which is similar to 'to order' in English. However, Norwegian often uses the infinitive form of the verb more frequently than English, and the word order can be more flexible. Be careful not to directly translate English phrases like 'I would like' as they are not commonly used in Norwegian. Instead, Norwegians often use simpler, more direct phrases.
rule: To order food in Norwegian, use the phrase 'Jeg vil ha...' (I would like...) followed by the item you want. The verb 'å bestille' can also be used, but it is more formal. For example, 'Kan jeg bestille...' (Can I order...). Remember that Norwegian word order is generally Subject-Verb-Object (SVO), similar to English, but with more flexibility in informal speech.

title: På apoteket / At the Pharmacy
bridge: In Norwegian, unlike English, the word for 'pharmacy' is 'apotek' (pronounced ah-poh-tehk). When asking for medication, Norwegians often use the verb 'å få' (to get) instead of 'to buy'. Be careful with false friends like 'resept' (prescription), which is pronounced similarly to the English word but has a slightly different spelling and emphasis.
rule: To ask for something at the pharmacy, use the phrase 'Kan jeg få...?' (Can I get...?). For prescriptions, say 'Jeg har et resept på...' (I have a prescription for...). Remember that Norwegian word order is similar to English, but adjectives often come after the noun. For example, 'en stor pakke' (a big package).

title: Å handle i butikken / Shopping at the Store
bridge: In Norwegian, asking for items in a supermarket is straightforward, but be aware that the word order is slightly different from English. Norwegian uses a more literal translation for 'Can I get...?' as 'Kan jeg få...?' which directly means 'Can I get...?'. Also, Norwegian speakers often omit the subject 'I' in casual speech, so you might hear 'Kan jeg få melk?' or simply 'Får jeg melk?' which can be confusing for English speakers.
rule: To ask for items in Norwegian, use the phrase 'Kan jeg få...?' followed by the item you want. For example, 'Kan jeg få melk?' means 'Can I get milk?'. If you want to ask if they have something, use 'Har dere...?' followed by the item. For example, 'Har dere brød?' means 'Do you have bread?'. Remember that Norwegian word order is similar to English, but the verb often comes second in questions.

title: Å kjøpe billett / Buying a Ticket
bridge: In Norwegian, buying a ticket for public transport often involves using a travel card or app, unlike in English where you might say 'buy a ticket'. Be careful with the verb 'å kjøpe' (to buy), as it's irregular and changes to 'kjøper' in the present tense. Also, note that 'billett' is singular in Norwegian, while 'tickets' is plural in English.
rule: To talk about buying a ticket in Norwegian, use the phrase 'å kjøpe billett'. The verb 'å kjøpe' is irregular and conjugates as follows: 'jeg kjøper' (I buy), 'du kjøper' (you buy), 'han/hun/den kjøper' (he/she/it buys), 'vi kjøper' (we buy), 'dere kjøper' (you all buy), 'de kjøper' (they buy). Use 'en billett' for one ticket and 'to billetter' for two tickets.

title: Å presentere seg selv / Introducing Yourself
bridge: In Norwegian, introducing yourself involves a more direct approach compared to English. While English often uses 'Nice to meet you' or 'Pleased to meet you,' Norwegian typically uses 'Hallo, jeg heter...' (Hello, my name is...). Additionally, Norwegians often include their surname, which is less common in casual English introductions. Be cautious not to overuse 'vel' (well) as it’s not a direct equivalent to 'well' in English introductions.
rule: To introduce yourself in Norwegian, use the phrase 'Hallo, jeg heter [name].' For example, 'Hallo, jeg heter Anna.' If you want to include your surname, add 'etternavnet mitt er [surname].' For instance, 'Etternavnet mitt er Hansen.' This structure is straightforward and polite, suitable for both formal and informal settings at the A1 level.

title: Bestille kaffe / Ordering Coffee
bridge: In Norwegian, ordering coffee is straightforward, but be aware of the word order and the use of 'en' or 'ei' for indefinite articles, which don’t exist in English for uncountable nouns like coffee. Also, Norwegians often use 'vær så snill' for 'please,' which is more formal than the casual 'please' in English.
rule: To order coffee in Norwegian, use the structure: 'Kan jeg få [coffee type], vær så snill?' For example, 'Kan jeg få en kaffe, vær så snill?' Note that 'en' is used for masculine nouns like 'kaffe' and 'ei' for feminine nouns. Always end with 'vær så snill' for politeness. If you want to specify size or additions, add them after the coffee type, e.g., 'en stor kaffe med melk.'

title: Å snakke i telefon / Talking on the Phone
bridge: In Norwegian, unlike English, the verb 'å snakke' (to talk) is commonly used for phone conversations, while 'å ringe' means 'to call'. Be careful not to confuse 'å ringe' with the English 'to ring', which in Norwegian means 'å ringe på døren' (to ring the doorbell). Also, Norwegians often use the phrase 'På telefonen' to indicate they are on the phone, which is more specific than the English 'on the phone'.
rule: To express talking on the phone in Norwegian, use the verb 'å snakke' followed by 'i telefonen' or 'på telefonen'. For example, 'Jeg snakker i telefonen' means 'I am talking on the phone'. To say 'Can I call you?', use 'Kan jeg ringe deg?'. Remember, 'å ringe' is the verb for 'to call', not 'to talk'.

title: Nødhjelp / Emergency Phrases
bridge: In Norwegian, emergency phrases often use the verb 'å trenge' (to need) instead of 'å behøve' as in some other languages. Be careful with word order in questions, as Norwegian typically places the verb second in main clauses, unlike English. Also, note that Norwegian uses the 24-hour clock, so mentioning time in emergencies differs from English.
rule: To express emergencies, use 'Jeg trenger hjelp' (I need help) or 'Kan du hjelpe meg?' (Can you help me?). For specific situations, add details like 'Jeg er skadd' (I am injured) or 'Ring 113' (Call 113). Questions follow the V2 word order (verb second), e.g., 'Kan du ringe etter en ambulance?' (Can you call an ambulance?). Always use the 24-hour clock for time references.
